items.title: Athar: a standard for service fingerprints
items.summary: Describe a service once, then convert it for every search engine and scanner. Gameel Ali, who works with me on Athar, recently shared queries on LinkedIn for finding ARTEX instances. ARTEX is the web console of an AI-driven, autonomous penetration-testing framework. It is deployed under many brand names: ARTEX, AntiFox, NKW, SHRIKE and others. I asked him how to run the same hunt on another platform. He replied with the query for that platform. Same hunt, different syntax. This is one title search for ARTEX on three engines: FOFA title="自主渗透测试控制台" Shodan http.title:"自主渗透测试控制台" Censys host.services.endpoints.http.html_title=~".*自主渗透测试控制台" So I asked: can’t we describe the fingerprint of these services once, in a generic format, and convert it into the queries of the different online services? A few hours later came the next idea. If a rule can become a search query, it can also become a Nuclei template or an Nmap NSE script. Then scanners can use the same fingerprints, not only search engines. That is Athar. Athar at a glance: a rule on the left, the athar CLI on the right. I’ve seen this problem before Nine years ago Thomas Patzke and I started Sigma for the same reason. Every SIEM had its own query language, and every detection idea was rewritten by hand for each of them. Sigma describes a log signature once, in YAML, and converters turn it into the query language of the SIEM you use. Today others carry the standard, and I’m more of an advisor: Thomas, Nasreddine Bencherchali, François Hubaut, Christian Burkard and Swachchhanda Shrawan Poudel do most of the work. Service fingerprints have the same problem today. A hunt gets published three or four times, once per search engine, as hand-written query strings. Those strings drift apart. They break when an engine changes its syntax; Censys deprecated its Legacy Search in September 2026. And nobody can test them. The principle is simple: describe a service once in a generic form, then convert it into the specific form each tool or service needs. It made sense for log signatures then. I think it makes sense for service fingerprints now. Describe a service once . Convert it for every engine and scanner. A rule If you can read a Sigma rule, you can read an Athar rule. The metadata and the detection block are Sigma. New are target, identifies, confidence and tests. title: Agentic Offensive Framework - ARTEX family target: protocol: http detection: selection: http.title|contains: 'Autonomous Penetration Testing Console' condition: selection identifies: family: artex category: offensive-tool confidence: high tests: - name: ARTEX console response: http.title: 'ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console' expect: match - name: Pentest vendor page response: http.title: 'Penetration Testing Services | Example Corp' expect: no_match Every brand of the console keeps the phrase “Autonomous Penetration Testing Console” in its title, so one condition finds all the rebrands. The real rule also matches the Chinese and Korean titles and reads the brand name out of the title. Two things matter here. A rule describes properties of a response, never engine syntax. Engine syntax lives in the converters, so when an engine changes its query language, we fix one converter, not every rule. And every rule carries tests: a response it must match and a near miss it must not. athar verify runs them, and CI rejects a rule whose tests fail. The athar CLI athar is a single Go binary. The rules are the only thing its commands share. athar convert turns rules into queries for FOFA, Shodan, Censys, ZoomEye, Modat Magnify and urlscan.io. Engines differ in what they can express, so every query carries a label. exact means the same results as the rule on that engine's data. approximate means the same intent with a looser operator, for example a whole-word match. superset means the engine can't express part of the rule, so the query drops that part and can only return more hosts, never fewer. Notes say what was lost and why. athar convert on two ARTEX rules: one query per engine, each with its label and notes. The same command writes Nuclei templates and an Nmap NSE script, so you can run the rules in the scanner you already use. Nuclei running converted Athar templates against local services that answer like an ARTEX console, an NKW rebrand, PentAGI and a Strix viewer. athar scan probes hosts you own or are allowed to test. Give it rules, hosts or CIDR ranges, and ports. It collects the TLS certificate, the response to GET /, the favicon and the banner, and prints one line per service that matches a rule: what it is, the brand it extracted, how confident the rule is, and the rule's author. athar scan -r rules/ -p 80,443,8787 10.0.0.0/24 athar scan on two live consoles on 25 November 2026: an ARTEX console, and an ARGOS rebrand that the family rule finds by its title. athar match is planned, not built yet. It will run rules over data you already have, such as engine exports or stored responses, without sending a packet. Its main job is to remove the over-matches of approximate queries: run a loose query on an engine, filter the export with athar match, and keep only what the rule really describes. Behind all three is one idea: the scanner defines what a rule means, not the engine query. scan and match use the same evaluator, so a query can be loose without making the results wrong. Have a look The first use case is the infrastructure of agentic offensive frameworks like ARTEX: AI-driven pentest consoles that keep changing their names. The format isn’t limited to them. C2 panels, phishing kits, appliances and ordinary server software fit the same way. Athar is a community project and a draft standard, so the rule format can still change. The rules are licensed under the Detection Rule License 1.1, the licence of the Sigma rules. The slide deck walks through the problem, a rule, the CLI and a real ARTEX hunt. Slide deck: the problem, a rule, the CLI and a real hunt for the ARTEX family. https://www.figma.com/deck/tFRGgSho2sEiq8mjW9pif8 Repository: https://github.com/Athar-HQ/Athar Latest release: binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows. https://github.com/Athar-HQ/Athar/releases/latest If you hunt infrastructure, send us your hunts as rules. You don’t have to write the YAML by hand: give your query and one host it found to an AI coding agent in the repository, and AGENTS.md tells it how to turn the query into a tested rule. And if something is missing, open an issue.

Describe a service once, then convert it for every search engine and scanner.

Gameel Ali, who works with me on Athar, recently shared queries on LinkedIn for finding ARTEX instances. ARTEX is the web console of an AI-driven, autonomous penetration-testing framework. It is deployed under many brand names: ARTEX, AntiFox, NKW, SHRIKE and others.

I asked him how to run the same hunt on another platform. He replied with the query for that platform. Same hunt, different syntax. This is one title search for ARTEX on three engines:

FOFA     title="自主渗透测试控制台"
Shodan   http.title:"自主渗透测试控制台"
Censys   host.services.endpoints.http.html_title=~".*自主渗透测试控制台"

So I asked: can’t we describe the fingerprint of these services once, in a generic format, and convert it into the queries of the different online services?

A few hours later came the next idea. If a rule can become a search query, it can also become a Nuclei template or an Nmap NSE script. Then scanners can use the same fingerprints, not only search engines.

That is Athar.

Athar at a glance: a rule on the left, the athar CLI on the right.I’ve seen this problem before

Nine years ago Thomas Patzke and I started Sigma for the same reason. Every SIEM had its own query language, and every detection idea was rewritten by hand for each of them. Sigma describes a log signature once, in YAML, and converters turn it into the query language of the SIEM you use. Today others carry the standard, and I’m more of an advisor: Thomas, Nasreddine Bencherchali, François Hubaut, Christian Burkard and Swachchhanda Shrawan Poudel do most of the work.

Service fingerprints have the same problem today. A hunt gets published three or four times, once per search engine, as hand-written query strings. Those strings drift apart. They break when an engine changes its syntax; Censys deprecated its Legacy Search in September 2026. And nobody can test them.

The principle is simple: describe a service once in a generic form, then convert it into the specific form each tool or service needs. It made sense for log signatures then. I think it makes sense for service fingerprints now.

Describe a service once. Convert it for every engine and scanner.A rule

If you can read a Sigma rule, you can read an Athar rule. The metadata and the detection block are Sigma. New are target, identifies, confidence and tests.

title: Agentic Offensive Framework - ARTEX family
target:
  protocol: http
detection:
  selection:
    http.title|contains: 'Autonomous Penetration Testing Console'
  condition: selection
identifies:
  family: artex
  category: offensive-tool
confidence: high
tests:
  - name: ARTEX console
    response:
      http.title: 'ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console'
    expect: match
  - name: Pentest vendor page
    response:
      http.title: 'Penetration Testing Services | Example Corp'
    expect: no_match

Every brand of the console keeps the phrase “Autonomous Penetration Testing Console” in its title, so one condition finds all the rebrands. The real rule also matches the Chinese and Korean titles and reads the brand name out of the title.

Two things matter here. A rule describes properties of a response, never engine syntax. Engine syntax lives in the converters, so when an engine changes its query language, we fix one converter, not every rule. And every rule carries tests: a response it must match and a near miss it must not. athar verify runs them, and CI rejects a rule whose tests fail.

The athar CLI

athar is a single Go binary. The rules are the only thing its commands share.

athar convert turns rules into queries for FOFA, Shodan, Censys, ZoomEye, Modat Magnify and urlscan.io. Engines differ in what they can express, so every query carries a label. exact means the same results as the rule on that engine's data. approximate means the same intent with a looser operator, for example a whole-word match. superset means the engine can't express part of the rule, so the query drops that part and can only return more hosts, never fewer. Notes say what was lost and why.

athar convert on two ARTEX rules: one query per engine, each with its label and notes.

The same command writes Nuclei templates and an Nmap NSE script, so you can run the rules in the scanner you already use.

Nuclei running converted Athar templates against local services that answer like an ARTEX console, an NKW rebrand, PentAGI and a Strix viewer.

athar scan probes hosts you own or are allowed to test. Give it rules, hosts or CIDR ranges, and ports. It collects the TLS certificate, the response to GET /, the favicon and the banner, and prints one line per service that matches a rule: what it is, the brand it extracted, how confident the rule is, and the rule's author.

athar scan -r rules/ -p 80,443,8787 10.0.0.0/24
athar scan on two live consoles on 25 November 2026: an ARTEX console, and an ARGOS rebrand that the family rule finds by its title.

athar match is planned, not built yet. It will run rules over data you already have, such as engine exports or stored responses, without sending a packet. Its main job is to remove the over-matches of approximate queries: run a loose query on an engine, filter the export with athar match, and keep only what the rule really describes.

Behind all three is one idea: the scanner defines what a rule means, not the engine query. scan and match use the same evaluator, so a query can be loose without making the results wrong.

Have a look

The first use case is the infrastructure of agentic offensive frameworks like ARTEX: AI-driven pentest consoles that keep changing their names. The format isn’t limited to them. C2 panels, phishing kits, appliances and ordinary server software fit the same way.

Athar is a community project and a draft standard, so the rule format can still change. The rules are licensed under the Detection Rule License 1.1, the licence of the Sigma rules.

The slide deck walks through the problem, a rule, the CLI and a real ARTEX hunt.

items.title: FIFA Alleged Breach – Hackers Claim Access to 12.2 GB of Sensitive Internal Documents
items.summary: FIFA has confirmed that hackers gained unauthorized access to a limited set of personal and business information. The Switzerland-based world football governing body has not confirmed a claim by the Handsome Boy Hacking Club (HBHC) that it obtained and published 12.2 GB of sensitive internal documents. The breach is confirmed, but the group has not verified the size or contents of the archive it claims to have released. A FIFA spokesperson told The Record on November 25 that the organization was working with relevant authorities, including law enforcement. FIFA condemned the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data. It did not answer the outlet’s follow-up questions about the incident. FIFA has not said how the hackers got in, when it detected the intrusion, or whose information was affected. In a November 21 post on X, Dark Web Informer said HBHC claimed to have taken files from FIFA’s Microsoft environment and internal governance systems. The group described the material as identity and immigration documents, information about executives, financial and legal records, and internal governance files and screenshots. Dark Web Informer said the claim was unverified. The group advertised the files for download and warned that some folders could contain corrupted or duplicate data. That makes the claimed archive size a poor measure of the breach’s impact. FIFA Alleged Breach A large archive can contain multiple copies of the same document, and its size does not show how many people were affected. The Record also reported that HBHC claimed it tried to extort FIFA before posting the files on a cybercrime forum. No public confirmation shows that FIFA’s files were encrypted. The group’s reference to a Microsoft environment does not identify a product or explain how the intruders got access. It does not establish that a Microsoft software flaw was involved or that any specific service, such as SharePoint, was breached. FIFA has not publicly named the affected systems. FIFA allegedly breached, 12.2 GB of sensitive internal documents leaked The Handsome Boy Hacking Club (HBHC) claims to have released data stolen from FIFA, the international governing body of football, headquartered in Switzerland. The group claims the files were extracted… pic.twitter.com/5X03OEZo2o — Dark Web Informer (@DarkWebInformer) November 21, 2026 If Microsoft cloud services were involved, audit logs could help investigators check for unusual sign-ins and see which files an account opened or downloaded. Cyber Security News previously covered the Microsoft cloud logging playbook , which explains how those records can help trace suspicious activity. The key question for affected people is whether their documents were among the files accessed or copied. In a November 23 statement, Spain’s LaLiga said an attacker stole personal data from a fan services platform between November 14 and 16. The platform served people registered with LaLiga and some clubs. The league said it blocked the attacker on November 16, notified Spain’s data protection agency and reported the incident to the National Police. It said the attack did not affect its other systems or disrupt the competition. No public evidence links the LaLiga incident to the FIFA breach. The two incidents involve different kinds of records. LaLiga identified a platform that held fan data. At the same time, FIFA has confirmed access to personal and business information without saying whose records were involved. Cyber Security News also previously reported on fake FIFA websites that collected personal information . That was a separate scam, not evidence that FIFA’s own systems had been breached. Anyone who receives an unexpected message asking them to upload identity documents in response to the breach should verify the request through an official channel before sharing anything. items.summary: Nothing in security is trickier than insider risk , because the person triggering it is already logged in, already permitted, and often acting in good faith the resignee copying files and the sloppy uploader set off identical alarms. The solutions below separate on where they center detection (user behavior, data movement, or analytics), whether they tell malice from carelessness, and how proportionately they can be run. Proofpoint takes 1 ; Microsoft and Forcepoint complete the podium. Key Takeaways • 1 overall: Proofpoint the people-centric ITM benchmark. • Podium: Proofpoint, Microsoft (M365-native Purview), Forcepoint (risk-adaptive enforcement). • Model split: user-centric monitoring (Proofpoint, Teramind, DTEX) versus data-centric (Varonis) versus analytics-centric UEBA (Gurucul). • 2026 theme: proportionality the programs that work pair strong detection with governance that keeps employee trust intact. How We Scored (Methodology) Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Criteria: detection approach (user, data, analytics), behavioral context (intent vs accident), data-movement visibility, forensic depth, privacy/proportionality controls, and pricing clarity. Weights: behavioral context 25% , data-movement visibility 25%, detection approach 20%, forensic depth 15%, proportionality controls 15%. Proofpoint — Best People-Centric ITM Benchmark Proofpoint — Best People-Centric ITM Benchmark Snapshot: Enterprise | ITM (ObserveIT lineage) with context | People-centric lens Why it earns 1: Proofpoint’s ITM captures user activity with context screen, file, and application timeline centered on the people most likely to pose or attract risk, inside its people-centric security program. For organizations wanting insider risk in the same lens as their email and data defense, it sets the benchmark. Pros: Activity capture with context; timeline forensics; people-centric lens. Cons: Endpoint-agent footprint. Bottom line: The people-centric ITM benchmark. 2. For Microsoft-stack estates, insider risk arrives without a new agent or vendor. Pros: Native M365 signals; policy templates; HR connectors. Cons: Value concentrates in the Microsoft stack. Bottom line: Insider risk native to Microsoft 365. 3. Forcepoint — Best Risk-Adaptive Enforcement Forcepoint — Best Risk-Adaptive Enforcement Snapshot: Enterprise | Risk-adaptive protection | Behavioral scoring + DLP Why it ranks here: Forcepoint scores user behavior continuously and dials enforcement up or down in response, tightening automatically as behavior drifts toward exfiltration. For programs wanting DLP that responds to intent rather than blanket-blocking, it’s the risk-adaptive pick. Pros: Risk-adaptive enforcement; behavioral scoring; integrated DLP. Cons: Tuning investment to calibrate scoring. Bottom line: DLP that responds to intent. 4. DTEX Systems — Best Behavioral-Analytics Lens DTEX Systems — Best Behavioral-Analytics Lens Snapshot: Per-user | Privacy-conscious behavioral analytics | Lightweight telemetry Why it ranks here: DTEX centers human-behavior analytics with a privacy-respecting, lightweight model building behavioral baselines and surfacing intent without heavy surveillance. For programs wanting analytics-led insight with proportionality built in, it’s the behavioral pick. Pros: Behavioral baselining; privacy-conscious telemetry; intent scoring. Cons: Deep session-forensics versus the UAM specialists. Bottom line: The privacy-conscious behavioral lens. 5. Teramind — Best Forensic User Monitoring Teramind — Best Forensic User Monitoring Snapshot: Per-seat tiers | Granular UAM + session playback | Forensic depth Why it ranks here: Teramind goes fine-grained keystroke, screen, application, and session capture with policy alerts and forensic replay the depth you want when an investigation must reconstruct exactly what someone did. For forensic-grade monitoring (with proportionality controls), it’s the UAM pick. Pros: Granular UAM; forensic playback; policy automation. Cons: Monitoring depth demands proportionality governance. Bottom line: The forensic-depth monitoring lane. 6. Mimecast (Code42) — Best Data-Exfiltration Detection Mimecast (Code42) — Best Data-Exfiltration Detection Snapshot: Per-user | Code42 Incydr within Mimecast | Exfiltration focus Why it ranks here: Code42 ’s Incydr, now under Mimecast, is purpose-built to catch file exfiltration across endpoint, cloud, and email with little policy setup. Buyers searching “Code42” evaluate the Mimecast product. For data-movement detection, it’s the exfiltration pick. Pros: Exfiltration detection; low-policy model; broad egress coverage. Cons: Confirm packaging within Mimecast. Bottom line: File-exfiltration detection, Mimecast-backed. 7. Varonis — Best Data-Centric Defense Varonis — Best Data-Centric Defense Snapshot: Enterprise | Permissions mapping + data-access anomalies | Data-first Why it ranks here: Varonis starts from the asset who can access what data, who actually does, and when access patterns go anomalous catching over-permissioning and exfiltration that user-watching tools miss. For data-first organizations, it’s the data-centric anchor. Pros: Permissions mapping; data-access anomaly detection; DSP breadth. Cons: User-behavior forensics versus the UAM tools. Bottom line: The data-first insider benchmark. 8. Gurucul — Best UEBA Analytics Gurucul — Best UEBA Analytics Snapshot: Enterprise | ML UEBA across identities and data | Risk scoring Why it ranks here: Gurucul applies ML UEBA across identities and data, scoring insider risk through behavioral baselines and anomaly detection spanning on-prem and cloud. For analytics-first programs, it’s the UEBA pick. Pros: ML UEBA; identity analytics; risk scoring. Cons: Model tuning and data onboarding. Bottom line: The UEBA-centric insider lane. 9. Netwrix — Best Audit-and-Governance Lane Netwrix — Best Audit-and-Governance Lane Snapshot: Tiers | Data-access auditing + change tracking | Governance focus Why it ranks here: Netwrix offers data-access auditing and change tracking through a governance lens, fitting organisations that anchor insider oversight on access audit. For audit-led programs, it’s the governance pick. Pros: Access auditing; change tracking; governance reporting. Cons: Behavioral-analytics depth versus the leaders. Bottom line: The audit-and-governance lane. 10. Veriato — Best SMB Behavioral Monitoring Veriato — Best SMB Behavioral Monitoring Snapshot: Per-user | User-activity monitoring + behavioral analytics | SMB fit Why it ranks here: Veriato delivers user-activity monitoring and behavioral analytics at economics suiting smaller organizations wanting insider visibility without enterprise platforms. items.summary: State-backed hackers and financially motivated groups are using ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework, to find exposed systems, steal credentials, and break into enterprise networks and cloud environments. In a November 25 report, Microsoft warned that the framework can move from scanning to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on the target’s defenses and how the operator uses it. The report does not describe a new exploit or a flaw in an AI model. Instead, ARTEX speeds up familiar techniques and reduces the need for an operator to intervene between steps. In one case, an AI agent went from searching public GitHub repositories for application secrets to extracting data from Azure Key Vault, Microsoft’s cloud service for storing secrets, in five minutes. Microsoft Threat Intelligence researchers identified six threat actors using ARTEX: Storm-0940, Storm-3358, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Crystal Typhoon, and Salt Typhoon. As earlier coverage of internet-exposed AI hacking frameworks showed, these tools can support authorized security testing, but the same automation can also speed up intrusions. ARTEX divides work among several AI agents. A planner reviews what the framework has discovered, workers carry out assigned tasks, and a reporter documents confirmed findings. The framework updates a shared record of systems and findings as work progresses. That matters because an agent can act on a discovery while other tasks are still running, rather than waiting for a person to review the results. Microsoft’s ConnectWise supply chain investigation found that China-aligned Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate intrusions. The ConnectWise Microsoft 365 campaign involved stolen application credentials and sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 customer environments, not 2,250 confirmed breaches. In multiple Storm-0940 intrusions, Microsoft observed the group reach privileged cloud access less than three hours after initial targeting. items.title: 4,000+ Servers Running AI Hacking Agents Are Exposed to the Internet and Actively Attacking
items.summary: The Shadowserver Foundation found around 4,200 internet-exposed instances of AI hacking frameworks on November 23, 2026, up from just under 3,700 a day earlier. Its November 25 report also documented more than 10,000 events from over 80 IP addresses identified as running these tools between November 9 and 23. The larger figure measures exposure. The smaller one counts sources that sent traffic to Shadowserver’s honeypots. The findings do not show that all 4,200 instances were attacking. Exposed AI Attack Framework instances per region – linear scale (source : Shadowserver) Shadowserver scans the internet daily for 15 AI attack frameworks and tracks exposure on its public dashboard. These tools use large language models to guide tasks such as finding exposed services and testing for known flaws with limited human input. 4,000+ Servers Expose AI Hacking Agents Security teams can use them for authorized testing. A public instance alone does not tell researchers who runs it or whether its activity is approved. Exposed AI Attack Framework instances per country (source : shadowserver ) ARTEX accounted for around 70% of exposed instances on most days. AntiFox, a version based on ARTEX, grew from a handful of instances to around 200. Together, they made up about three-quarters of observed instances on November 22. A jump in PentestCode deployments helped drive the next day’s increase. Nearly half of the exposed instances were in Asia, more than a third were in North America, and most of the rest were in Europe. Nearly nine in ten attacking IP addresses were fingerprinted as ARTEX Gateway (source : shadowserver ) The FBI’s November 13 advisory said some ARTEX-assisted intrusions moved from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. In a separate case, Cyber Security News reported on a CyberStrikeAI intrusion that exposed 3,392 user accounts. Those cases show what the tools can do in real intrusions. Shadowserver’s honeypot data measures attempted activity, not confirmed breaches. Honeypots are decoy systems that record suspicious traffic. Nearly nine in ten source IP addresses seen by Shadowserver were identified as running ARTEX Gateway. Half of the IP Addresses Tried to Relay Traffic (source : Shadowserver) A handful generated most of the events, and the busiest address was linked to PentAGI. Almost all sources were on cloud networks. Activity was concentrated in the United States and Hong Kong, but that likely reflects where the servers were hosted, not where the operators were based. About six in ten source addresses tried to relay traffic through the sensors. Direct requests often probed VPN gateways, web apps, and developer tools such as Jenkins. About one in ten source addresses sent exploit or injection attempts, most often targeting the Metabase flaw CVE-2023-38646 . Some also looked for .env files, which can contain database passwords and cloud API keys. The focus on known flaws echoes earlier reporting on ARTEX attacks . VPNs, Web Apps and Developer Tools were the Main Targets (source: Shadowserver) Shadowserver recommends checking its free Device Identification report for the ai-attack-framework label. If a deployment is approved, limit access to trusted addresses or a VPN, require strong authentication, and keep the software updated. If no one can verify that the deployment is approved, isolate it and investigate possible misuse. Most sources operated in short bursts, but a few sent traffic during every hour of the day over several days. Shadowserver advises teams to rate-limit repeated probes and make sure alerts are handled outside business hours. Mostly Short Bursts, But Some Ran Around The Clock (source: Shadowserver) Before blocking an address, check it against recent logs. Cloud IP addresses can be reassigned, and an old report may no longer describe the system using that address. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

items.title: Roundcube Webmail Flaws Could Let Hackers Execute Malicious Code and Expose Sensitive Data
items.summary: Roundcube released Webmail versions 1.6.22 and 1.7.7 on November 23, 2026, to address 12 security flaws. The updates fix weaknesses in how the browser-based email client handles attachments, displays messages, and connects to mail servers. The release notes describe flaws that could expose data and allow unauthorized email filter code to run . However, they do not confirm remote code execution on the webmail server or report active exploitation of these bugs. One fix stops Roundcube from passing unsafe PDF, PostScript, and SVG attachment content to ImageMagick, a tool used to process images. Roundcube had previously attempted to fix this issue. The project also revisited an HTTP request injection flaw in its ATD spellcheck backend, which could allow unintended requests. The release notes do not say which configurations are most at risk or whether either flaw could give an attacker control of the server. Several fixes address how Roundcube displays HTML email. Two flaws let message styling break out of the limits meant to keep it separate from the webmail interface. Another let SVG content load external resources despite the user’s remote-content settings, weakening a privacy control that helps prevent email tracking. Roundcube Webmail Flaws The update also closes a flaw that could expose responses handled by the CSS proxy. It fixes a gap in the HTML filter on systems running PHP versions earlier than 8.4. Two separate flaws could let unauthorized instructions enter Sieve scripts, which mail servers use to run rules such as sorting incoming messages. Another fix addresses XML injection in the XIMSS driver of Roundcube’s password plugin. The release also closes a denial-of-service flaw where the decoder for TNEF attachments, a format associated with Microsoft Outlook, could spend too long processing attachment data. The updates also stop Roundcube from falling back to unencrypted IMAP, SMTP, or ManageSieve connections when TLS encryption is configured. However, the mail server does not advertise the required capability. That matters because a setting that appears to require encryption did not always prevent an unencrypted connection. Administrators should back up their data and patch production systems promptly. The official Roundcube 1.6.22 release notes identify it as the final release in the 1.6 long-term support branch. Teams that cannot move to 1.7 immediately should apply 1.6.22 rather than wait for the migration. The Roundcube 1.7.7 release notes list the same security fixes, and Roundcube says only the 1.7 branch will receive future security updates. Cyber Security News previously covered CISA’s warning about exploited Roundcube vulnerabilities and a separate Roundcube flaw that let attackers track email opens . Those reports concern earlier bugs, not the flaws fixed in November. They offer two reasons to keep webmail current: attackers have targeted Roundcube before, and a flaw does not have to take over a server to compromise user privacy. For teams still on 1.6, this update closes the current gaps, but moving to 1.7 is what keeps future fixes available. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. items.title: What Two Million Canary Prompts Reveal About AI Supply Chain Security
items.summary: Executive Summary To evaluate the security of the AI supply chain, Dragos seeded approximately two million AI prompts with canary URLs and credentials. The investigation revealed that prompt data was stolen from at least three AI hosting providers and from the system of a Chinese AI lab, which accessed secret URLs from prompts marked for zero data retention. No security team can audit the providers its prompts pass through, whether they are foreign or domestic. Every team can test its own side: the models it calls and what goes into each prompt. Qualys TotalAI maps the models and AI services in use, red-teams any model with a chat completion endpoint (including foreign models), and detects secrets before they reach a prompt. Inside the Canary Experiment In a study published on November 19, 2026 , a team from Dragos, led by Chief Research Officer HD Moore, sent approximately two million prompts to popular AI services from July through November, tracing around 2,000 request routes. Each prompt carried canary tokens: unique URLs and live AWS keys linked to empty accounts that were fully monitored. If a URL was accessed, it indicated that the system had read the prompt; if a key was used, it showed that someone had stolen a credential. What the Dragos Canary Study Exposed Breached Providers Attackers have stolen prompt data from at least three AI hosting providers, and Dragos reports that these providers were unaware of the breaches until they were notified. In the largest breach, every canary request Dragos sent during several late-October windows was stolen. This included requests that the provider had rejected before any models had a chance to run. Attackers tested the AWS keys, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, attempted to enable Amazon Bedrock models, create Bedrock API keys, and add IAM users. One adversary later used ARTEX, an LLM-driven penetration testing framework, to confirm that the keys were active. Leaky Routes AI routers forward requests to pools of hosting providers, and every hop can access the full prompt. A Zero Data Retention (ZDR) setting is intended to ensure that the service an application calls does not retain prompts or responses, yet Dragos found ZDR-marked requests stolen or scraped further down the route. They also discovered instances of marketplace sellers logging prompts and a router quietly forwarding some traffic to these marketplaces. A Foreign Lab Reading Flagged Prompts A Chinese AI lab’s systems fetched secret URLs from more than half of the prompts sent to its models, including about two-thirds of those marked ZDR; U.S. resellers of its models triggered the same scraper. In a later statement, the lab said an internal security monitoring process extracted and probed the URLs, and that it has disabled that process for forwarded API traffic. Providers Cannot Be Audited. The Customer Side Can Be Tested. Every finding turned on one fact: whatever sits in a prompt, from a live credential to customer data or source code, can be seen by every hop on the route. A credential turns that exposure into an intrusion. No model test can show what a provider’s infrastructure does with a request. Security teams can only test their own systems, and Qualys TotalAI answers four questions about this. 1. Which Models and Routes Are in Use? Qualys TotalAI leverages existing Qualys sensors. Cloud Agents and scanners can fingerprint AI software and GPUs, cloud connectors map managed AI services, Container Security covers AI workloads, and a browser plug-in shows workforce AI usage. Qualys Container Runtime Security adds evidence about where containerized AI applications connect. Security teams can correlate DNS and outbound TCP events from monitored workloads to track direct connections to AI routers or provider endpoints outside their approved list. For requests routed through a provider, they can use router or gateway records to identify the reported inference provider. Qualys TotalAI enhances this visibility by testing supported model endpoints for sensitive information disclosures. Self-hosting, which Dragos recommends where affordable, takes third parties off the route but makes the model server the target. Qualys detects known vulnerabilities and default credentials in servers such as Ollama, vLLM and LiteLLM, and AI detection and response (AI-DR)¹, an extension of Qualys EDR to AI assets, is designed to catch attacks on that infrastructure as they happen. 2. Do The AI Models In Use Leak Their Context? Red-team tests show what a model gives away under attack. TotalAI evaluates any model with a chat completion endpoint , including foreign models, against 300+ attack scenarios mapped to OWASP , MITRE ATLAS , and the EU AI Act, including 21 sensitive information disclosure checks. A model that discloses a real credential from its system prompt, retrieved documents or tool output proves it sat in the model’s context, where every hop could see it. When a test fails, automated guardrail remediation¹ is designed to push the fix into Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. 3. Can a Secret Reach the Prompt? Guardrails control what a model repeats, not what it was sent: in the largest breach, attackers stole some requests rejected before any model ran. The test that matters is whether a secret can reach the prompt at all, and that starts where secrets live. Qualys scanning detects exposed secrets in container images, CI/CD pipelines, and code repositories. This leak class was responsible for a provider notice in November, where an AI coding agent committed a credential to a public repository. TotalAI MCP scans test the servers that agents source context from for credential exposure. Additionally, MCP tool-call tracing¹ is designed to show what each tool call passes into an agent’s context. Secrets also enter at run time, pasted by users or returned by tools, where static scans cannot see them. Policy-based runtime controls with inline blocking¹ are designed to block or redact secrets before a request exits the organization. A key that never reaches the first hop cannot be stolen further down the route. 4. What Can a Stolen Key Reach? Qualys analysis of a 2026 intrusion traced an exposed AWS key to a complete cloud takeover in under ten minutes. TotalCloud CIEM shows what each cloud identity can access and flags excess privileges. Its posture checks cover AI services such as Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker, and Azure OpenAI. TruRisk Insights AI attack paths¹ are designed to connect exposed endpoints, excess permissions, and sensitive data into one prioritized path. What to Do This Week Map the models and routes in use. Flag any connection to a router or provider that no one approved, as well as any self-hosted model server that can be reached without authentication. Test the models in use, including foreign ones, after every change to a model or prompt. Find secrets in code, images, and agent context. Remove them before an agent can load them. Rotate secrets in prompts covered by any provider or router notice, and give agents short-lived, least-privilege keys. Hunt for the indicators. Search CloudTrail for ARTEX user agents artex-agent and artex-judge-r121 , Bedrock enablement, new Bedrock API keys, and new IAM users. Dragos also recommends pinning providers and verifying Zero Data Retention on every hop. Test the Models No One Can Audit The Dragos study found no new class of vulnerability: exposed credentials and broken privacy promises, moving through a supply chain customers can barely see. No team can audit the provider side. Every team can test the models it calls and keep secrets out of the prompt. Learn how to map your AI in use, test its models, and catch secrets before they reach a prompt. Start Your 30-Day Free Trial Organizations already running Qualys Cloud Agents have a first AI inventory waiting, with no separate AI security agent to deploy. Key Takeaways Treat any secret that has appeared in a prompt as exposed. A privacy flag is a promise from one hop, but a prompt crosses several. Providers cannot be audited from outside, but models can be tested and the first hop mapped. Test whether a secret can reach the prompt. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What did the Dragos canary study find? From July through November 2026, Dragos sent about two million prompts carrying canary URLs and AWS keys to AI services. It found prompt data stolen from at least three AI hosting providers, marketplace sellers logging prompts, and a Chinese AI lab’s systems fetching secret URLs from prompts marked for zero data retention. Can security teams test AI models they do not host? Yes, for model behavior: TotalAI tests any model with a chat completion endpoint, including foreign models. What a provider’s infrastructure does with a request is outside what any model test can see. Does Zero Data Retention protect AI prompts? Zero Data Retention (ZDR) protects a prompt only at the hop that honors it. In the Dragos study, ZDR-flagged requests were stolen inside breached providers, and their secret URLs fetched downstream. Security teams should verify the route as well as the settings, including what each hop’s retention terms exempt from. What is AI supply chain security? AI supply chain security means controlling every service that handles an organization’s AI traffic: models, routers, inference providers, and the agents that build each prompt. How should organizations secure self-hosted AI models? Treat model servers such as Ollama, vLLM and LiteLLM like any other exposed service: patch known vulnerabilities, remove default credentials and require authentication on every API. Qualys publishes detections for specific issues with Ollama, vLLM, and LiteLLM. ¹ Features expected to be available by the end of Q4 2026. Product features, functionality, and release dates may change at any time at Qualys’s sole discretion.

items.title: Make post-quantum cryptography updates routine with AWS-LC
items.summary: As your organization plans upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), you should also think about cryptographic agility to more easily update algorithms used to protect your data. Changes to cryptography and related protocols aren’t new, but PQC is accelerating the pace at which organizations must add new algorithms and remove old ones to keep up with changing regulations and evolving business risk. AWS believes our key to success is standardizing on one cryptographic library that embodies three key properties: compatibility, assurance, and performance. In this blog post, you’ll learn how we think of the cost and friction of ongoing cryptographic updates in terms of these properties. You’ll learn how AWS built AWS-LC to embody these properties, thus making cryptographic upgrades straightforward and low-impact for ourselves and our customers. For custom applications where you can’t yet use AWS services and must operate your own stacks, this post also shares why you might consider using AWS-LC as your standardized library. Every cryptographic algorithm used to protect your data today has an expiration date, even if no regulator has set one yet. Algorithms that were once the standard, such as MD5 and SHA-1, have been retired. Standards are revised and flaws are found in implementations. The move to post-quantum cryptography is the current wave of changes, with dates set by governments and regulators to complete the transition. PQC itself will progress in phases to enable hybrid and pure post-quantum algorithms and then deprecate traditional cryptography. Each change reaches your systems as a software library update, so the practical question is how often you can roll out a new version of your cryptographic library, and what each rollout costs. At AWS, we think of this cost in terms of three properties. Compatibility means an update doesn’t require application changes. Assurance means new code can be trusted when it ships, without a long bake period. Performance means a new algorithm doesn’t add so much computational overhead or latency that it gives teams a reason to wait. This post describes how AWS-LC provides each property, and how you can apply the same approach to the cryptography you own. AWS-LC is the general-purpose cryptographic library that AWS maintains and uses across its services. It is derived from BoringSSL, which originated from OpenSSL. If you’ve called an AWS API, AWS-LC was used on the server side. Through s2n-tls, it provides hybrid post-quantum key exchange on AWS service endpoints and in services like Application Load Balancer and Network Load Balancer . It’s also the cryptography under aws-lc-rs for Rust, the default provider for rustls , and under the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider for Java. Because so much of AWS depends on one library, we built it to be updated often. AWS-LC keeps an OpenSSL-compatible API so applications can replace algorithms without a rewrite. It uses formal verification to prove selected algorithm implementations correct. It optimizes algorithm implementations to reduce the latency and compute costs that new algorithms add. The same properties work outside AWS. For example, 1Password used AWS-LC to move its clients to hybrid post-quantum key exchange with no application code changes. Hand off what you can, standardize what you keep Each piece of cryptography you own is one more thing to change at every transition. By owning as little of your cryptographic stack as your constraints or requirements allow, and using AWS services to manage the rest, you can minimize your ongoing responsibility and operational risk. If your workload relies solely on managed services like AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) and managed resources like Elastic Load Balancer or Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) , you’re already reaping the benefits of AWS-LC and the AWS shared responsibility model. You only need to keep your clients and resource configurations updated. As your organization plans upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), you should also think about cryptographic agility to more easily update algorithms used to protect your data. Changes to cryptography and related protocols aren’t new, but PQC is accelerating the pace at which organizations must add new algorithms and remove old ones to keep up with changing regulations and evolving business risk. AWS believes our key to success is standardizing on one cryptographic library that embodies three key properties: compatibility, assurance, and performance. In this blog post, you’ll learn how we think of the cost and friction of ongoing cryptographic updates in terms of these properties. You’ll learn how AWS built AWS-LC to embody these properties, thus making cryptographic upgrades straightforward and low-impact for ourselves and our customers. For custom applications where you can’t yet use AWS services and must operate your own stacks, this post also shares why you might consider using AWS-LC as your standardized library.

Every cryptographic algorithm used to protect your data today has an expiration date, even if no regulator has set one yet. Algorithms that were once the standard, such as MD5 and SHA-1, have been retired. Standards are revised and flaws are found in implementations. The move to post-quantum cryptography is the current wave of changes, with dates set by governments and regulators to complete the transition. PQC itself will progress in phases to enable hybrid and pure post-quantum algorithms and then deprecate traditional cryptography. Each change reaches your systems as a software library update, so the practical question is how often you can roll out a new version of your cryptographic library, and what each rollout costs. At AWS, we think of this cost in terms of three properties. Compatibility means an update doesn’t require application changes. Assurance means new code can be trusted when it ships, without a long bake period. Performance means a new algorithm doesn’t add so much computational overhead or latency that it gives teams a reason to wait. This post describes how AWS-LC provides each property, and how you can apply the same approach to the cryptography you own.

AWS-LC is the general-purpose cryptographic library that AWS maintains and uses across its services. It is derived from BoringSSL, which originated from OpenSSL. If you’ve called an AWS API, AWS-LC was used on the server side. Through s2n-tls, it provides hybrid post-quantum key exchange on AWS service endpoints and in services like Application Load Balancer and Network Load Balancer. It’s also the cryptography under aws-lc-rs for Rust, the default provider for rustls, and under the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider for Java. Because so much of AWS depends on one library, we built it to be updated often. AWS-LC keeps an OpenSSL-compatible API so applications can replace algorithms without a rewrite. It uses formal verification to prove selected algorithm implementations correct. It optimizes algorithm implementations to reduce the latency and compute costs that new algorithms add. The same properties work outside AWS. For example, 1Password used AWS-LC to move its clients to hybrid post-quantum key exchange with no application code changes.

Hand off what you can, standardize what you keep

Each piece of cryptography you own is one more thing to change at every transition. By owning as little of your cryptographic stack as your constraints or requirements allow, and using AWS services to manage the rest, you can minimize your ongoing responsibility and operational risk.

If your workload relies solely on managed services like AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) and managed resources like Elastic Load Balancer or Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS), you’re already reaping the benefits of AWS-LC and the AWS shared responsibility model. You only need to keep your clients and resource configurations updated. Many organizations can rely on AWS to provide the infrastructure and basic automation, but still own and manage the endpoints and applications where most of the work happens. For these components, it’s helpful to standardize on as few cryptographic libraries as possible. With fewer libraries, your team learns each one well: how to configure it, run it, and update it. The library you standardize on also decides how often you can update it. If an update requires application changes, ships new code that no one trusts yet, or adds compute and latency, teams have a reason to wait. In the rest of this post, we show you how AWS-LC removes each of those reasons through compatibility, assurance, and performance.

Compatibility

The best library update is one that doesn’t impact your application and that your users don’t notice. Code changes happen at three points: adopting a library, adding an algorithm, and updating the library. AWS-LC keeps each one small.

  • Adopting AWS-LC  – For TLS, AWS-LC libssl keeps an OpenSSL-compatible API, so most applications that use OpenSSL for TLS build against it with small changes. Applications that call libcrypto directly might need more work, because the AWS-LC libcrypto API differs from OpenSSL’s in places. See the porting guide for where behavior differs.
  • Adding an algorithm  – When new algorithms are added in AWS-LC behind interfaces applications already call, s2n-tls, s2n-quic, aws-lc-rs, and the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider adopt them automatically. Hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, for example, is enabled through existing TLS configuration APIs. For 1Password, that meant a one-line Cargo.toml change and no application code changes.
  • Updating the library – AWS-LC long-term support (LTS) releases keep a stable application binary interface (ABI). Applications link once, then take library updates without a rebuild. One update reaches every application on the host when each process restarts. The Amazon Linux 2027 preview uses this method to ship AWS-LC as a system library.

We built these properties so AWS services could move to AWS-LC with minimal effort. aws-lc-rs is also used by open source projects; it’s the default cryptography provider for rustls with over 100 million downloads in the past 90 days, CPython tests against AWS-LC in continuous integration, and HAProxy publishes packages built on it. Each new use surfaces problems earlier in the update process, and every fix is recorded in one codebase.

Assurance

Every new algorithm arrives as new code, and new code is where bugs and security vulnerabilities are usually found. If you can’t trust new code when it ships, you wait, and each wait delays the next change. Tests check the inputs you run, and proofs check every input. AWS-LC uses machine-checked proofs for its most critical code, including its post-quantum algorithms and parts of its classical algorithms, such as its 25519 elliptic-curve code.

AWS-LC contributes to and takes its ML-KEM and ML-DSA code from two open source projects: mlkem-native and mldsa-native. The algorithmic implementations in these projects already incorporate formal verification safeguards such as ensuring no out of bound memory access, no integer overflows, constant assembly run time, and functional correctness using tools like CBMC and HOL Light (for more information, see Verifying and optimizing post-quantum cryptography at Amazon). AWS-LC imports this code from upstream without changing it. The proofs don’t depend on instruction order, so the assembly can be re-optimized without redoing them. That prevents verification from becoming the reason a faster implementation waits. Other cryptographic implementations of the library are verified in s2n-bignum.

We use these proofs alongside testing and FIPS validation. For workloads that require FIPS 140-3, a validated module is required to allow new code to be deployed. AWS-LC FIPS 3.0 was the first cryptographic library to include ML-KEM in a FIPS 140-3 validation. ML-DSA, the NIST post-quantum signature standard (FIPS 204), is in the AWS-LC FIPS 4.0 module, and the FIPS 5.0 module includes the faster, formally verified mldsa-native implementation. Both have been submitted to NIST for validation.

Performance

A new algorithm that costs more to run gives teams a reason to delay, and across many connections a small cost per connection adds up. AWS-LC optimizes each algorithm it adds so that cost doesn’t delay the update. Amazon Science reports 2.0 to 2.4 times more ML-KEM operations per second than the reference implementations across Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance types. Earlier work applied the same approach to 25519 elliptic-curve cryptography. The optimized code is covered by the proofs described in the previous section, so speed doesn’t reduce assurance.

ML-DSA followed the same path. AWS-LC moved from its original implementation to mldsa-native, with optimized assembly for AArch64 and x86_64 platforms, and it now signs and verifies faster on both Graviton and x86 EC2 instance types. As a result, compute is no longer the main cost of post-quantum signatures: in the measurements in the following section, we show that ML-DSA-44 certificates lowered average TLS handshake latency compared with RSA-2048. What remains is size, which the next section measures.

What it costs to move

AWS services handle billions of requests every second, so anything that could affect those requests must be carefully considered. Post-quantum cryptography impacts the performance of every new TLS connection, so before we adopted ML-KEM and ML-DSA, we invested heavily in making them fast. Figure 1 shows the resulting reduction in time for both key exchange and authentication. Today, moving to PQ confidentiality has no net cost for most AWS use-cases, and PQ authentication takes less compute than the RSA certificates we use today.

Figure 1. ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-87 time per handshake, before and after AWS-LC’s native implementations, on AWS Graviton4

ML-KEM-768 key exchange decreased by over 50 percent on both the client and the server (as shown in Figure 1); we described how in Verifying and optimizing post-quantum cryptography at Amazon. In this post, we’re focusing on ML-DSA. In AWS-LC v1.49.1, ML-DSA used the original AWS-LC implementation, adapted from the reference code. In v5.10.0, it runs on mldsa-native, which implements the performance-critical kernels in hand-written Arm64 Neon assembly for AWS Graviton, including: the number-theoretic transform (NTT) and its inverse, tuned for Arm cores with the SLOTHY superoptimizer, along with pointwise multiplication, rejection sampling, and the decompose, hint, and norm-check steps of signing and verification. It also expands the public matrix four entries at a time using the AWS-LC four-way parallel SHA-3 (Keccak). These optimizations, as shown in the right half of Figure 1, reduced ML-DSA-87 signing time on the server and verification time on the client, and the same assembly is covered by the formal proofs described earlier. mldsa-native is open source, part of the PQ Code Package in the Linux Foundation’s Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance (PQCA), and the AWS Cryptography team and Amazon Automated Reasoning Group contribute to it.

Figure 2. TLS 1.3 connection setup time by algorithm, between two AWS Graviton4 hosts in the same Availability Zone

Figure 2 shows total handshake time for various configurations, when the client and server are in the same AWS Region. For a baseline, we used TLS performance when the server prioritized ECDHE with P-256 for key exchange and RSA-2048 certificates for authentication. With the optimizations to ML-KEM, there is negligible overhead from moving to hybrid ML-KEM key exchange (the second bar from left). The hybrid key exchange preferred in AWS systems today pairs X25519 with ML-KEM-768. X25519 is faster than P-256, and that saving covers the remaining ML-KEM work, so a full connection setup takes roughly 12 microseconds more, which doesn’t meaningfully impact throughput or latency. It’s worth noting here that ML-KEM-768 introduces approximately 2.3 KB to the handshake.

PQ authentication carries more risk, because authentication is more of the handshake cost. The server signs once for each handshake, and the client verifies three signatures: the server’s handshake signature, the signature on the leaf, and the signature on the intermediate certificate. RSA-2048 signing is expensive and verification is inexpensive. ML-DSA-87 reverses that balance, shifting some work from the server to the client.

ML-DSA keys and signatures are also much larger, so the server’s handshake messages grow from 4–7 KB to 17–24 KB depending on the chosen certificate parameters. That adds certificate parsing on the client and more data to encrypt and send on the server. Within an Availability Zone, those messages still arrive in one round trip, and we measured no difference in network time between configurations.

Compared to RSA 2048, which is still prevalent today, ECDSA offers faster processing. However, both must be replaced by ML-DSA for post-quantum authentication. With the optimizations in AWS-LC, ML-DSA-44 comes close to ECDSA, and every ML-DSA parameter set is significantly faster than RSA-2048, as shown in Figure 2. As a result, we’re confident in managing the performance impact from migrating to post-quantum certificates.

Another facet of our investments in reducing performance impact is session resumption. Handshake costs apply only to new connections. Session resumption reduces how often that cost is paid. A resumed TLS 1.3 handshake authenticates with a key from the earlier session and sends no certificates or signatures, so the larger ML-DSA keys and signatures apply only to full handshakes. We’ll note here that in psk_dhe_ke mode, the resumed handshake still runs a fresh hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, which preserves forward secrecy. Now, resumption only helps if the client can present its ticket to any server behind the endpoint, so AWS has been extending support for resumption across the hosts behind its service endpoints. AWS SDKs can reuse connections across many requests, and session resumption can skip certificates and signatures entirely, which gives the most performance benefit for workloads using AWS managed services. If you’re using AWS-LC directly in your own custom applications, consider keeping session tickets enabled, prefer TLS 1.3 with psk_dhe_ke, and reuse clients so that they keep their tickets between connections.

Conclusion

Every cryptographic choice has an expiration date, so the goal isn’t to pick the right algorithm once and never replace or update it, but to make each replacement routine. Start by handing off what you can to AWS services and standardizing what you keep on as few libraries as possible. For the cryptography you own, three properties decide how quickly and how often you can implement each update. For compatibility, new algorithms arrive behind the APIs your applications already call, and long-term support releases keep a stable ABI, so adopting one takes a library update and a restart, not a rebuild. For assurance, machine-checked proofs cover a library’s most critical code, ML-KEM is inside a FIPS 140-3 validated module, and ML-DSA is in modules submitted for validation. For performance, optimized implementations keep each new algorithm from adding compute or latency that might give teams a reason to wait. Post-quantum cryptography is the change in front of us now, and it won’t be the last.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

Josh Williams

Josh is a Software Engineering Manager in AWS Cryptography, where he leads the team that builds AWS-LC. His team’s work spans post-quantum algorithms, formal verification, and performance optimization. He previously led teams in AWS Networking and Amazon Aurora DSQL and brings broad experience in ecommerce and distributed systems.

Jake Massimo

Jake is an Applied Scientist on the AWS Cryptography team, where he bridges Amazon with the global cryptographic community through active participation in international conferences, academic research, and standards organizations. His work focuses on advancing the adoption of post-quantum cryptographic technology at cloud scale. Currently, he leads the development of optimized and formally verified post-quantum algorithms within the AWS cryptographic library.

Rohit Panjala

Rohit is a Senior Security Specialist at AWS, driving go-to-market (GTM) strategy on a global scale for AWS data protection services, including keys, certificates, secrets, and post-quantum cryptography. He brings 7 years of experience in cybersecurity and cloud, with a background in security product management at IBM and electrical engineering.

items.summary: A would-be spy is recruited on Telegram for $15,000 and sent halfway around the world to snoop on Palantir. His cover story when he's caught? He wanted to ask a woman out on a date. Meanwhile, Carl Miller investigates a think tank with 300 experts on its books, one of whom is the inconveniently dead Henry Kissinger. But who is its real audience? You might be surprised. Plus, Coreview's Andrea Sivieri explains why Microsoft Copilot is brilliant at finding anything in your company, including the salary spreadsheet someone shared with everybody back in 2019. All this and more in episode 494 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Carl Miller.
